description:
Houston, We Have AI!

Two university friends, one mission, and probably way too much AI. We're a duo of developers from Tashkent, Uzbekistan, passionate about coding, AI, space, and turning crazy ideas into working projects. Powered by Python, caffeine, questionable sleep schedules, and unlimited ambition.

Houston, the problem isn't AI. It's what we're about to build.
summary: Lunar Lab is a 3D strategy game in which young explorers build a lunar base, manage interconnected life-support resources, and use a rover to investigate a fictional polar landscape. Interactive lessons introduce controls and scientific reasoning through game actions. Learners interpret NASA observations, build power and life-support systems, and organize rover expeditions and supply deliveries. The game is an educational simulation, not an engineering design or astronaut certification tool.
details:
Keeping a lunar crew alive is a systems problem: electricity, water, oxygen and food depend on one another. In Lunar Lab, the player places and powers modules, manages supplies, sends a rover to investigate sites, and responds to changing mission conditions. A visible 3D assembly frame follows actual construction progress and stops when the game is paused; raw material collected by the rover must return to the base before treatment. Commander Academy contains six guided missions: Rover and map, Data and solar power, Science expedition, Relay expedition, What should we build first?, and equipment delivery from Earth. In the fifth lesson, learners choose whether to build solar power or oxygen production first, place and construct both actual modules, and compare battery, oxygen and water outcomes over two simulation stages. They can replay the other order without overwriting their saved campaign. The consequences come from the shared game model: oxygen production consumes water and electricity, while solar generation supplies power rather than oxygen. The coefficients and resulting numbers are illustrative game values, not NASA measurements or an operational optimization recommendation. In the sixth lesson, learners compare two landing locations with different drivable routes and identify an occupied location that cannot be used. They select a pad, dispatch a purchased equipment kit, watch its flight progress and physical cargo-rover journey, then install the delivered solar module and see its power output. Landing alone does not add the equipment to inventory. Pause and replay let learners compare the choices without changing their saved campaign. The lesson explicitly compresses flight time by four; routes, distances, costs, cargo and timing are game values, not NASA mission measurements. Loading is an instantaneous handoff. NASA’s Lunar Landing & Launch Pads provides context on landing hazards and pad concepts; the game does not simulate rocket-plume physics, regolith ejecta or a validated landing-safety model. In the communication mission, a rover loses contact behind terrain; the player establishes a relay and transmits data before returning to the saved base. The lunar globe provides a mission-selection view using a NASA SVS lunar texture. Earth supply flights offer a choice between consumables and equipment for longer-term autonomy. After landing, a separate cargo rover physically carries the purchased cargo to the base; resources are credited only after arrival and when storage permits. Blocked routes can be replanned without losing the paid cargo. Loading into the carrier is simplified, not a simulated robotic unloading sequence. The exploration rover separately returns crater material for treatment. Players can deploy a field camp after the rover reaches a remote site; the camp lowers nearby survey and sample-operation costs. It is a rover-deployed facility, not a separately controllable mobile construction vehicle.

The interface supports Russian and English, mouse and touch input, a collapsible tactical map, a direct rover-selection control, and reopening a visited site from its marker. Module activity indicators and machinery animation follow the simulation’s computed working, limited or idle state; they do not invent production. Pausing lets learners plan without consuming resources. Saved progress preserves construction, exploration and paid deliveries. Soft original music and action cues provide feedback; audio is presentation, not sound propagating through lunar vacuum.

NASA evidence informs interactive activities. Players distinguish the temperature background and observed water-ice signatures in the Moon Mineralogy Mapper composite from an LROC map showing how frequently the lunar south pole was illuminated during a six-month observation period. They also examine a historical solar flare record from NASA DONKI and radiation measurements from NASA OSDR RadLab. The latter were taken aboard Orion and are not a measurement of the lunar surface. These exercises ask players to read evidence and avoid conclusions that the data do not support. DONKI and RadLab are interactive archived-data interpretation exercises: players calculate the flare duration, compare instrument readings, and assess what the observations can and cannot establish. They do not drive a radiation simulation in the campaign.

Terrain, mission sites, resources, coefficients and game outcomes are fictional or simplified. They illustrate concepts and must not be interpreted as NASA measurements or operational forecasts. The intended audience is children and teenagers; learning outcomes have not been established by a user study.
